scoreNote: Between Adequate and Strong (4.5): correctly grants the reason a partial truth and shows it does not justify the claim, since imagination needs experience to be worth anything; clear and well organized, if it could press the point a little harder.

sentences.text: We celebrate the visionary who imagines what has never been, and we sometimes pity the veteran weighed down by the way things have always been done.
The claim that imagination is more valuable than experience rests on the reason that those who lack experience are free to imagine the possible, unconstrained by established habits and attitudes.

The reason contains a kernel of truth, but it does not justify the claim, because imagination and experience are not rivals but partners, and experience usually strengthens imagination rather than caging it.

sections.role: Body — The reason is partly true

sentences.text: First, the reason rightly notes that inexperience can sometimes free the mind.
A newcomer is not yet bound by the assumptions that long practice quietly instills, and may imagine a solution that veterans have stopped believing is possible.
Outsiders have indeed transformed fields precisely because they did not know which ideas were supposed to be off limits.
Experience can harden into habit, and habit can blind even the talented to alternatives they no longer think to consider.
So the reason is not baseless: a lack of experience can, on occasion, be a kind of freedom.

sections.role: Body — But it does not justify the claim

sentences.text: However, that inexperience sometimes frees imagination does not make imagination more valuable than experience.
Imagination without experience is mostly idle fantasy, since experience is what tells us which imagined possibilities are worth pursuing and how to make them real.
A child can imagine a city on Mars, but only experienced engineers and scientists could begin to build one; the vision is empty without the knowledge to realize it.
The great innovators we admire were rarely ignorant dreamers; they were people who imagined boldly because they understood their field deeply enough to see where it could go.
Experience also feeds imagination, supplying the raw material — the problems, patterns, and possibilities — from which new ideas are actually built.
Far from being imagination's rival, experience is usually its fuel and its guide.
A vision no one yet knows how to build is, by itself, just a wish.
An imagination with nothing to work on imagines nothing worthwhile.
Moreover, the reason mistakes the rare case for the rule.
For every outsider whose fresh imagination succeeded, countless inexperienced dreamers imagined the impossible and achieved nothing, because they lacked the experience to tell vision from delusion.
The constraints of established habits the reason scorns are often hard-won lessons about what does not work, not mere prejudice to be ignored.
The most valuable mind is not the inexperienced one free to imagine anything, but the experienced one that can imagine and judge at once.
The veteran's caution is often experience quietly whispering what the dreamer cannot yet hear.
Freedom from experience is freedom from knowledge, which is no advantage at all.
In conclusion, the reason is partly true but the claim does not follow from it.

Inexperience can occasionally free the imagination, but imagination needs experience to become anything more than daydreaming, so the two are partners and neither is simply more valuable than the other.
The most powerful asset is not imagination over experience, but imagination informed by it.
